claims.text: The magnetocaloric response of nanoscale non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys is dominated by interfacial strain.
Modified magnetic-domain configurations alter the magnetostructural coupling observed in bulk FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys.
The enhanced interface-to-volume ratio of thin films and nanoribbons increases domain-wall pinning and immobilization.
Increased domain-wall pinning amplifies magnetic hysteresis.
Increased domain-wall pinning reduces the effective magnetocaloric response under low applied fields.
As-deposited nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons have a disordered microstructure.
The as-deposited microstructure contains randomly distributed interface strains and domain-pinning centers.
Controlled thermal annealing relieves local interfacial strain.
Controlled thermal annealing produces a more uniform magnetic-domain structure.
Annealing-induced strain relief and domain reconfiguration decrease domain-wall pinning.
Decreased domain-wall pinning makes magnetostructural transitions more reversible.
More reversible magnetostructural transitions reduce magnetic hysteresis.
More reversible magnetostructural transitions improve the effective magnetocaloric response.
Annealed samples will have lower magnetic hysteresis than otherwise identical as-deposited controls.
Annealed samples will show a modest increase in effective low-field magnetocaloric response relative to as-deposited controls.
As-deposited films and nanoribbons have pronounced hysteresis and a diminished magnetocaloric response compared with bulk counterparts.
The predicted annealing effects occur within a temperature window near the magnetostructural transition.
The predicted mechanism applies under low fields on the order of tens of millitesla and when heat transfer is not the primary cycle-rate limitation.
Intrinsic heat-transfer rates limit magnetic-cooling cycle frequency.
At very high fields or in bulk-like geometries, mechanisms other than interfacial strain and domain-wall pinning may govern the response.
